turn_text: Sure. Yeah, it is. The first thing you have to look at any bill that you look at is good for the nation. Is it good for my state? Is it good for my district? My priorities have been, and they switch over time as different issues come up. Right now, I sit on the Appropriations Committee and trying to get the Appropriations process working again, trying to get the bills approved so that agencies know what their funds are going to be available. and to hold them accountable for the funds that we have given them that they're doing their job as efficiently as they can. I chair the Interior Subcommittee that has Bureau of Land Management, the Forest Service, all the rest of the Department of Interior, the Bureau of Indian Affairs, the Geological Survey, the Smithsonian, things like that. We have a lot of undocumented workers that have worked here for years and years in the agricultural industry, because frankly, no one else will take the jobs. They actually have to apply to try to get American workers to fill some of these jobs. And there's not American workers that will take a lot of these jobs. So we depend on these foreign workers, if you will. But a lot of them have been here for a number of years. They're undocumented. But they're a part of our society, like anybody else. We need to make this a legal process for them. And with the legislation that we've been looking at, we want them to come out of the woodwork. paid taxes, all that kind of stuff, paid penalty coming here illegally and so forth. But let them participate in society and stuff. So that's, we've got a number of Republicans and Democrats working together to try to pass this bill. We've passed it in the House and the last two Congresses haven't been able to get through the Senate yet, but we're still working on that. But I think if we can address that, it will go a long ways towards solving some of the agricultural problems that we have across the country.

turn_text: There are things called community funding projects that used to be called earmarks, what we changed the name because earmarks got a bad name. I've always been a supporter of those because I think members of Congress know they're district better than anybody else. Now, if you're going to ask for stupid things to be funded, your name is going to be on the front page of the paper. And when people come to us because they go through our committee, some of them, we always ask them, you know, have you thought about what this is going to look like if this gets on the front page of your paper? If we do water and sewer systems in in my bill, well, somebody wants to do water system for say a golf course. People might look at that and go, do we really want to have our taxes being used to do a water system for a golf course that ought to be able to do their own water system, you know, And people think about that and they say, well, maybe that's not a good idea. But when you've got a community, like a rural community in Idaho that needs to improve their water system because they have to meet the clean drinking water standards and the clean water standards and the safe drinking water standards, those are federal laws. So we help them. with the resources necessary to rebuild their water systems to meet those standards because they don't have the resources to do it in a small community. And so a lot of the projects that we help fund or request funding for are to help those smaller rural communities and stuff. I'll give you the example, but I always use Firth Idaho, burn their fire station down accidentally. They've been operating for the last year and a half under their fire station has been operating in an abandoned potato cellar. That's not very good. And so they don't have the resources to rebuild their fire station and replace the fire engine and a few things like that that were damaged. They don't have the tax base to be able to do that. But yet, here's these 1,000 people in Firth and 30,000 people in the surrounding community, depending on the fire department. So we help them with a grant to help them fund rebuilding their fire station and stuff. To me, that's a perfectly legitimate thing. And I think it's important that some of these resources that our taxpayers in Idaho send to the federal government be used back in Idaho. So that's why we ask for these things. We have to list them. If you look at any bill that'll be on the back of the bill on who asked for what. And you can go at our home pages and see what we've requested in community finance projects. And then you got to convince 51 people over in the Senate. Well, the way they're rules are, you got to convince 60 people in the Senate that you're right. Then you got to convince the administration that you're right. And it is a laborious project to get something done. And people will say, well, government shouldn't be that hard to run. I wouldn't want a government that's easy to run. I wouldn't want a government where everybody that has a new idea can just make a law with it and stuff. It ought to go through the rigors of debate and having to convince other members that what you want to do is right. That's okay, but it's frustrating for people out there to go, oh man, you know, why can't Congress ever do anything and that kind of stuff? It's supposed to be hard, and it is. But it is, as I said, the most rewarding job I've ever had being able to represent the people of Idaho.

explicit_propositions.text: This job will be both the most exciting and frustrating experience a freshman will have.
It is expected and intentional that governing is difficult.
Ideas should undergo rigorous debate and persuasion before becoming policy.
Freshmen often believe they have the perfect solution to a problem upon arrival.
Representing the people of Idaho is the most rewarding job the speaker has ever had.
Convincing 218 people in the House is necessary to achieve consensus on legislation.
Convincing 51 people in the Senate is insufficient; at least 60 votes are required.
Getting things done in government is a laborious process.
The administration must also be convinced before action can occur.
A government that is too easy to operate would be undesirable.

assumptions.text: Effective governance requires broad consensus across multiple decision-making bodies.
Democratic deliberation depends on the ability of individuals to persuade others based on merit.
Frustration in policymaking stems from the legitimate complexity of democratic systems, not inefficiency.
The speaker values institutional rigor and procedural legitimacy over speed or convenience.
Complexity in governance protects against hasty or ill-considered policies driven by popular sentiment.
The public’s expectation of quick legislative action misunderstands the purpose of representative democracy.
The speaker identifies strongly with the role of representation and sees it as personally fulfilling.
Legislators are morally obligated to justify their positions to peers and constituents.
Public frustration with Congress reflects a lack of understanding about how democracy functions.
Trust in governmental outcomes increases when decisions require extensive justification and agreement.
